explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "we try to persuade men." Persuading means talking with people, not pushing them around. I think that's a gentle way to treat anyone you care about. And notice he says "try," which makes me feel better about the cookies I try to stamp straight.

Paul goes the other direction, friend. He writes, "we try to persuade men," and you can't persuade somebody you're hiding from. Avoiding people is what a junk drawer is good for, and I would know. Paul walks toward people and talks with them.
Good guess, but that's not the word in this verse. Paul writes, "we try to persuade men." Persuading is a conversation, and judging is a gavel. Paul picks the conversation.

Paul writes that some take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. Appearances are like a cookie that looks perfect on top and is raw dough in the middle. Pretty on the outside, nothing going on inside. Paul wants the Corinthians able to answer people who care only about what shows.

Money never comes up in this verse, friend. Paul says some take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. Appearances are what you can see from across the room. The heart is what only shows up when you spend time with a person.
Power sounds like a fair guess, but Paul doesn't say it here. The word is appearances. Some people take pride in how things look rather than in the heart. That's a frosting-only kind of pride.

Paul writes, "if we are of sound mind, it is for you." The "you" is the church in Corinth, the people he's writing to (2 Corinthians 1:1). So the passionate part is for God and the steady part is for them. I think that's a pretty generous way to describe your own behavior.

The Jerusalem church isn't in this verse. Paul says, "if we are of sound mind, it is for you," and he's talking to the church in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:1). The word "you" is the clue, friend. When a letter says "you," check the address on the envelope.

No rulers show up in this verse. Paul writes, "if we are of sound mind, it is for you," and the "you" is the Corinthians, the church he addressed in 2 Corinthians 1:1. This is a letter to church folks. He's talking to people he cares about.

Paul writes, "Christ's love compels us." Compels means it presses on him from the inside, like a pull he can't ignore. He doesn't say he was pushed from the outside. I think that's the difference between doing a job and doing it because you love the One you're doing it for.
That's a reasonable guess, but it's not the word Paul uses. He writes, "Christ's love compels us." Love is what moves him here. A command tells you what to do, and love makes you want to.
Power is a big word, but it isn't in this verse. Paul writes, "Christ's love compels us." What drives him is love. Not a muscle, friend, a heart.

Paul writes that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again. Living for yourself is a very small kitchen to bake in. The verse points you toward Christ instead. Notice that it says He was raised again, so the One they live for is alive.

Close, but the verse says something different. Paul writes that those who live should no longer live for themselves. Then he points to Him who died for them and was raised again. The blank is about turning away from yourself, not toward the world.

Rulers don't appear in this verse, friend. Paul writes that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again. The turn is from self to Christ. Nobody in between gets the credit.

Paul writes, "Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer." So there was a time he and the people with him saw Christ only through the flesh. Now they don't. That's a real change in how they see Him.

This one is true, friend. Paul writes, "Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer." The "way" he means is according to the flesh. So he really does say they once saw Christ that way, and then stopped.

Paul writes, "The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!" It doesn't say the old got a patch or a polish. It says it passed away. That's good news for anybody tired of being the old version of themselves.

I get why mended sounds nice, but Paul says something bigger. He writes, "The old has passed away." Not patched up, passed away. And when God makes something new, He means new, like He says in Revelation 21:5.
Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!" So the old doesn't stay put. The new has arrived, and that's the whole point of the verse.

Paul writes that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, "not counting men's trespasses against them." God isn't keeping a tally against them. Think of a big sheet of paper where the marks aren't being added up. That's good news for anyone who feels like their list is long.

Prayers aren't what this verse talks about. It says God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, "not counting men's trespasses against them." The word is trespasses. God isn't counting those against people.

Vows don't appear in this verse, friend. Paul writes that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, "not counting men's trespasses against them." Trespasses are the word. And God isn't counting them against anyone.

Paul writes, "He has committed to us the message of reconciliation." God put the message into their hands. I think that's quite a thing to be trusted with. It's even bigger than being trusted with the good cookie sheet.
That one is true, friend. Paul writes, "He has committed to us the message of reconciliation." So God did hand that message to them. It isn't kept in a locked cabinet.

Paul writes, "we are ambassadors for Christ." An ambassador speaks for the one who sent him, and he doesn't make up his own message. Paul adds that it's "as though God were making His appeal through us." So he and the people with him carry Christ's message.
Priests aren't in this verse, friend. Paul writes, "we are ambassadors for Christ." An ambassador carries a message for the one who sent him. That's the picture Paul chooses.
Nobody in this verse is a judge. Paul writes, "we are ambassadors for Christ." Israel isn't mentioned at all here. An ambassador speaks for the one who sent him, and that's all.

Paul writes, "We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God." Implore is a strong word, like a plea. I think you only plead like that when you really want someone to say yes. This is the message the ambassadors carry.

Faithful is a good word, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He writes, "We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God." The word is reconciled. That's the same word he used for what God has been doing.
Grateful sounds sweet, friend, but Paul's word is different. He writes, "We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God." Reconciled is the one. And he says implore, so he means it.

explanations.answer: So in Him we might become the righteousness of God
explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." Read it slowly and you see the two sides. The One who knew no sin was made to be sin on our behalf. Then "in Him" we become the righteousness of God. That's the text's reason, and I'll leave it as big as Paul wrote it.

explanations.answer: So in Him we might inherit the land of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason Paul gives, friend. He writes, "so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." Land isn't in this verse at all. The reason Paul states is about righteousness.

explanations.answer: So in Him we might keep the whole law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason here. He writes that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, "so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." The law of Moses isn't mentioned in the verse. The reason is right there in Paul's words.

Paul writes, "we urge you not to receive God's grace in vain." He says it as God's fellow workers, so he means it kindly. In vain means for nothing, like a cookie box that never gets filled. I think Paul wants the grace to count for something.
That's not what Paul warns about, friend. He writes, "we urge you not to receive God's grace in vain." Outsiders aren't mentioned in this verse. His worry is about receiving it in vain.

That one sounds like a warning Paul could give, but it's not in this verse. He writes, "we urge you not to receive God's grace in vain." The words are receive it in vain. He says it as God's fellow worker.
Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!" So he doesn't say it's a long way off. He says now.

Paul writes, "Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!" He says now, not someday. He's quoting words God says (Isaiah 49:8): "In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you." Paul takes those words and says now is the time.
